item.title: China aims to cement its place at forefront of biomedical innovation with new 5-year plan
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-18
China aims to cement its place at forefront of biomedical innovation with new 5-year plan BEIJING, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- China on Friday released a five-year plan for its pharmaceutical industry, outlining targets such as keeping biomedical research, development, and application at the global forefront by 2030. This move signals the country's resolve to turn drug innovation into a strategic strength. The plan, jointly issued by the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology and nine other authorities, calls for a major leap in the core competitiveness and international influence of China's pharmaceutical industry from 2026 to 2030. It is hoped that core technologies in key fields will see systematic breakthroughs during this period. Specifically, first-in-class drugs developed in China should account for no less than 25 percent of the global total, with the number of innovative drugs approved for market ranking among the world leaders. The innovative drug sector is expected to grow at an average annual rate of at least 20 percent, according to the plan. China also expects the biomedical sector to take shape as a national pillar industry at an accelerated pace. The combined revenue of pharmaceutical enterprises above a designated scale threshold -- an annual main business revenue of 20 million yuan (about 2.96 million U.S. dollars) -- should reach at least 3.5 trillion yuan by 2030, the plan says. The number of companies with an annual revenue exceeding 10 billion yuan should grow to 50. At least five Chinese drugs should achieve global annual sales exceeding 1 billion U.S. dollars, according to the plan. The plan arrives at a pivotal moment as China's pharmaceutical industry is shifting rapidly from its traditional identity as a supplier of active pharmaceutical ingredients and a large consumption market, toward a new phase defined by the export of innovative drugs. In the first half of this year, 38 innovative drugs were approved in China, of which 31, or more than 80 percent, were domestically developed. As of the end of 2025, China had 4,751 innovative drugs in the pipeline, accounting for one third of the global total and placing it first in the world for drugs under development. The broader industry also showed great vitality. Value-added output of China's pharmaceutical enterprises above the 20-million-yuan revenue threshold grew 6.4 percent year on year in the first half of this year. Moreover, China's innovative drugs have gained wider global reach. The total value of overseas licensing deals for innovative Chinese drugs has surpassed 120 billion U.S. dollars this year, up 36 percent year on year. Copyright © 2026 People's Daily Online. China's property market sees major changes in supply and demand: official (Xinhua) 13:06, September 18, 2026
BEIJING, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- China's property market has seen major changes in supply and demand and entered a new phase increasingly centered on existing housing stock, an official said Friday. The share of second-hand home transactions in total housing transactions rose from 27 percent in 2020 to 46 percent in 2025, and 52 percent in the first eight months of this year, said Zhang Xuetao, an official with the Ministry of Housing and Urban-Rural Development, at a press conference. A share exceeding 50 percent marks the property market's transition into the new phase, according to Zhang. (Web editor: Zhang Kaiwei, Liang Jun)

item.title: 95 years on, some in Japan still cling to militarist fantasies
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-18
95 years on, some in Japan still cling to militarist fantasies: Global Times editorial The erroneous claims concerning Taiwan made by three far-right Japanese scholars are a case in point that Japan completely disregards international norms and the principle of national sovereignty, and are heading down the historical path of militarist expansion abroad. The historic warning of the September 18 Incident still reverberates, and Japan is advised to turn back from its wrong path and win back the trust of its Asian neighbors and the international community through concrete deeds. This year marks the 95th anniversary of the September 18 Incident. As the world works together to uphold the outcomes of World War II victory and safeguard the postwar order in East Asia, Japan's right-wing forces are stirring against the tide, with their militarist ambitions on the rise. Recently, three right-wing Japanese scholars openly declared on a Japanese media program that they would "do whatever it takes to prevent Taiwan from falling into the hands of China." Such claims abandon historical conscience and academic integrity, turning gross interference in China's internal affairs into a matter of geopolitics. They expose an alarming reality: 95 years on, some in Japan still cling to militarist fantasies. The extreme remarks by the three scholars are not isolated incidents, but a reflection of the continued expansion of right-wing thought in Japan. The Takaichi cabinet has just completed a new round of personnel appointments for the ruling Liberal Democratic Party leadership and the cabinet, behind which lies a deeper plan by Japan's conservative camp to promote constitutional revision and military expansion. On the surface, the goal seems to be to stabilize the regime, strengthen governance, and control the Diet, but in reality, it is to consolidate conservative forces, clear internal obstacles and pave the way for breaking through the postwar framework and advancing constitutional revision and military expansion. From the continued conservative shift in Japanese politics to the spread of historical revisionism and the steady loosening of military constraints, a series of dangerous trends have once again sounded the alarm for regional security and stability. Tracing the root causes, Japan's current restlessness stems from the convergence of multiple factors: a deviation in value orientation, a distorted understanding of history, and misguided strategic judgment. Hijacked by right-wing ideology, Japan has gradually embraced "increasing military autonomy and projecting strength abroad" as the direction of its governance. The spirit of the pacifist constitution has been set aside, military expansion is equated with "national strength," interference in other countries' internal affairs is regarded as a "routine means" of geopolitical maneuvering, and the logic of regional coexistence is replaced by confrontational thinking. This distorted inversion of priorities continues to undermine the hard-won postwar peace order in East Asia. The severe distortion of historical understanding has left Japan mired in historical revisionism. Japanese right-wing forces deliberately try to cut the historical threads of modern East Asia, evade the aggressive nature of the September 18 Incident, and downplay or even whitewash the crimes of colonial rule and militarism. They refuse to confront their responsibility for aggression and evade reflection on the war, replacing historical justice with narrow nationalism. Through fragmented narratives, they seek to distort the established historical facts of World War II, attempting to undermine the foundations of Japan's postwar historical reckoning and fabricate a false historical narrative to justify military restrictions being loosened and overseas adventurism. Their strategic judgment has fallen into a distorted and dogmatic mindset, leading Japan to misread the currents of the times and the international landscape. Japan's right-wing forces, clinging to zero-sum thinking and the law of the jungle, mistakenly regard China's development as a "threat," treat regional peace as a chessboard for geopolitical rivalry, and fantasize about restoring regional advantages through external balancing, military expansion, and alignment with forces from outside the region. These misguided judgments, running counter to the general trend of the times, have prompted Japan to make one reckless choice after another that violates moral principles and damages relations with its neighbors, gradually pushing the country down a strategically dangerous path. Ninety-five years have passed since the September 18 Incident, but the militarist expansionist mindset that gradually took root in Japan since modern times and became deeply entrenched has yet to be fully eradicated. Yet rather than maintaining a sense of reflection on its history of aggression, Japan has allowed right-wing currents to grow and repeatedly crossed the red lines of the postwar international order. The erroneous claims concerning Taiwan made by the three scholars are a case in point that Japan completely disregards international norms and the principle of national sovereignty, and are heading down the historical path of militarist expansion abroad. Such voices are by no means isolated noise. They are an outward manifestation of the proliferation of right-wing thinking in Japan and also an inevitable consequence of the Japanese authorities' tolerance of historical revisionism and deliberate efforts to stoke a climate of confrontation and incite anti-China sentiment. More alarming than such rhetoric are Japan's concrete actions to systematically break free from the postwar framework of peace. Driven by right-wing forces, Japan has continued to sharply increase its defense budget, accelerated the development and deployment of offensive weapons, relaxed restrictions on the export of lethal weapons, and continued to hollow out Article 9 of its pacifist constitution. From military expansion and efforts to build momentum for constitutional revision to hyping perceived "security threats" in the surrounding region and coordinating with forces from outside the region, Japan has repeatedly abandoned its commitment to an "exclusively defense-oriented" policy and changed its postwar identity as a peaceful nation - Japan's "neo-militarism" is surging and posing a grave threat. Former Japanese Prime Minister Yukio Hatoyama once urged Takaichi to correct the mistake by quoting Confucius: "To make a mistake and not correct it - this is what is called truly making a mistake." A country that has neither settled nor shown sufficient willingness to settle the historical accounts of its past can never become a "normal country" in the true sense of the term. The historic warning of the September 18 Incident still reverberates, and Japan is advised to turn back from its wrong path and win back the trust of its Asian neighbors and the international community through concrete deeds. item.title: BRICS to write a new chapter of strength through unity for the Global South
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-18
BRICS to write a new chapter of strength through unity for the Global South From Sept. 12 to 13, Chinese President Xi Jinping attended the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi, India, where he delivered an important speech. He reviewed the achievements of BRICS cooperation over the past 20 years, called on BRICS countries to strive to be pioneers in four areas, and put forward five initiatives for deepening BRICS cooperation, charting the course for the high-quality development of greater BRICS cooperation. The international community closely followed Xi's attendance at the summit and spoke highly of China's important role in rallying the strength of BRICS, advancing BRICS cooperation, and promoting the development and revitalization of the Global South. This year marks the 20th anniversary of BRICS cooperation. Over the past two decades, the BRICS cooperation mechanism has continued to grow and expand, demonstrating strong vitality and becoming the most influential cooperation platform in today's world for emerging markets and developing countries. Today, unilateralism and power politics are on the rise, while multilateralism and the international order face mounting challenges. Deficits in peace, development, security, and governance continue to widen. Xi urged BRICS countries to stand firmly on the right side of history, strive to be a pioneer in advancing innovation-driven development, a pioneer in upholding peace and stability, a pioneer in facilitating mutual learning between civilizations, and a pioneer in reforming and improving global governance. He emphasized that BRICS countries should steer the international order in a direction that is more just and equitable, and work together to build a community with a shared future for humanity. As the world undergoes profound changes unseen in a century at an accelerating pace, the collective rise of the Global South has emerged as a key force driving the development of a more multipolar world. To make the world more stable and prosperous, BRICS countries must seize the initiative of history, unite the broader Global South, play a positive, stabilizing, and constructive role in international affairs, and promote the common well-being of humanity. At the Session II of the 18th BRICS Summit, Xi stressed that Global South countries should hold high the banner of multilateralism, uphold the authority and role of the United Nations, support multilateral institutions in advancing reform and increasing efficiency, and ensure the equal participation of all countries in international affairs. He further stated that they should see to it that the reform of the World Trade Organization proceeds in the right direction, uphold such principles as the most-favored-nation treatment, and actively explore new rules for the future. He said, "We should support the operation and development of the New Development Bank to facilitate Global South cooperation. The international financial architecture must be reformed and improved to increase the representation and voice of developing countries." Leaders attending the summit spoke highly of China's important contribution to the growth and development of the BRICS cooperation mechanism, saying that all sides should uphold the BRICS spirit, work to build a fairer and more inclusive international order, and create a secure and prosperous multipolar world. For greater BRICS cooperation to make greater contributions and achieve greater development, a solid foundation for practical cooperation is essential. The question is how the greater BRICS cooperation can leverage its strengths in emerging markets and its links with the Global South to build incubators for innovation, upgrade traditional industries, develop emerging industries and foster industries of the future. Xi proposed the open source and inclusive AI initiative, trade and investment facilitation initiative, digital industry cooperation initiative, intelligent manufacturing cooperation initiative and science and technology talent development initiative, charting the course for the high-quality development of greater BRICS cooperation. China will be a pioneer in establishing a BRICS AI open source community, support the cooperation in developing and applying large language models, hold specialized AI seminars and training courses, and build an open ecosystem for AI. China proposes to establish a BRICS special economic zone partnership, under which countries can set up an intelligent portal, coordinate policies, and build a new frontier for open development. China will push for establishing a BRICS digital ecosystem cloud platform, and conduct digital skills training, technological exchange and industrial alignment, so as to jointly enable the development of the digital economy. China proposes to set up a BRICS engineer cultivation alliance for joint development of engineers and mutual recognition of competency standards. These practical measures demonstrate China's firm commitment to advancing the development of greater BRICS cooperation in the spirit of openness, inclusiveness and win-win cooperation. Twenty years of trials and tribulations have shown that solidarity and cooperation have always been the source of strength for the cause of BRICS. China will take over the BRICS presidency next year and host the 19th BRICS Summit. It stands ready to work with all parties to build consensus and create a brighter future, usher in the third "Golden Decade" of BRICS cooperation, open up new prospects for prosperity and progress, and join hands to write a new chapter of strength through unity for the Global South. item.title: Three dimensions reveal what the Pinglu Canal brings to development
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-18
Three dimensions reveal what the Pinglu Canal brings to development The Pinglu Canal, China's first major river-to-sea canal project that has been planned and coordinated at the national level since 1949, is set to open for navigation on Sept. 16, 2026. What changes will this landmark project bring to the region? A closer look at the project from three dimensions -- economy, livelihoods, and environment -- offers a clear picture. Photo shows the Zicai Bridge over the Pinglu Canal. (Photo/He Guangmin) Economic benefits: injecting new vitality into regional development Once operational, cargo vessels will enter the canal at the mouth of the Pingtang River after passing Hengzhou in south China's Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region, then sail south to Qinzhou Port and out to sea. This will provide southwestern China with a more direct water route linking its inland regions to the ocean. The reduction in distance is significant. Goods shipped from southwestern China via the Pinglu Canal will travel approximately 560 kilometers less along inland waterways to the sea than those shipped via Guangzhou Port in Guangdong province. "Logistics costs are expected to fall by 18 to 30 percent, saving around 5.2 billion yuan ($774 million) in social transportation costs each year," said Cheng Yaofei, commander of the Pinglu Canal project construction headquarters. For an individual company, that means lower transportation costs. For an entire region, it creates opportunities for industrial relocation and reorganization. In 2025, the Pinglu Canal Guigang Economic Development Zone signed contracts for ten new projects with a combined investment of approximately 13.3 billion yuan. In Qinzhou, Shanghai Huayi, a Chinese chemical enterprise group, is developing an integrated chemical and new materials industrial base with a planned total investment of around 100 billion yuan. The company intends to use the canal to expand its markets and connect upstream and downstream businesses. Guangxi Jingui Pulp & Paper Co., Ltd. is also planning to build a terminal along the canal so that raw materials such as timber and calcite can be transported directly to its factories by water. Lower logistics costs are boosting the region's appeal for industrial clustering and creating new momentum for development. At the Liujing Port Area of Nanning Port in Nanning, capital of Guangxi, berths have been upgraded from handling 2,000-ton vessels to 5,000-ton vessels. Eleven river-sea intermodal berths at Qinzhou Port have also been upgraded. Cross-border transport routes, including the China-Laos Railway, are expected to connect with the inland waterway network as well. Wu Jian, director of the Institute of Regional Development at the Guangxi Academy of Social Sciences, noted that lower transportation costs are expected to attract industries, logistics, and producer services to cluster along the canal, while further strengthening industrial links between Guangxi and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area, and ASEAN. Photo shows the Madao water control hub of the Pinglu Canal. (Photo/Ji Haixin) Benefits for people -- enabling residents along the river to live and work in greater comfort The Pinglu Canal is not only changing the flow of goods; it is reshaping the lives of people living along its route. At a resettlement site in Shaping township, Lingshan county, Qinzhou, rows of neat townhouses stand alongside well-equipped public facilities, including a recreational square, a farmers' market, a kindergarten and a supermarket. A total of 13 centralized resettlement sites have been planned and built across Luwu, Jiuzhou, and Shaping townships in Lingshan county. So far, 1,498 households, representing 6,156 people, have been relocated, and all resettlement homes have been handed over to the residents. Chen Jidong, a relocated resident at the Shaping site, is very pleased with his new home. "In the past, the market and school were scattered around the village and quite far away. Now everything is within a few minutes' reach, making everyday life much more convenient," Chen said. His family has not only moved into a new home but also bought a truck. Chen previously made a living transporting materials at the Pinglu Canal construction site. "With the canal opening, there will be greater demand for transportation, so we have more to look forward to," he said. More local job opportunities close to home are reaching a growing number of residents. Thirty-four-year-old Huang Zhenjie has worked with the "Pinglu Employment" service program for over three years. He once helped a returned migrant worker secure a position as a steel bar worker at a canal construction site. After mastering the necessary skills, the worker now earns 12,000 yuan per month. "We not only recommend jobs, but also organize trial work and training," Huang said. So far, construction of the Pinglu Canal has created more than 70,000 job opportunities for local residents, with more than 2.6 billion yuan in labor remuneration. A child poses for a picture at the starting point of the Pinglu Canal in Pingtang village, Xinfu township, Hengzhou, south China's Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region. (Photo/Ji Haixin) Environmental benefits: protecting lucid waters and lush mountains through meticulous measures As the canal advances, environmental protection has kept pace every step of the way. Near the Qingnian water control hub, a 480-meter-long composite fish passage and a smart monitoring and assessment system have been put into operation. The Qingnian water gate, built in 1959, once obstructed fish migration. Today, a vertical-slot fishway and an eel passage have reconnected the waters upstream and downstream. Since the system began operating in 2025, its sonar monitoring system has recorded more than 76,000 fish swimming upstream and more than 115,000 swimming downstream, with over 10 species successfully completing their migration. Fish now have a passage for migration, and terrestrial animals have safe routes to cross the canal as well. Near the Madao water control hub, a 240-meter-long, 20-meter-wide wildlife overpass spans the canal. The bridge is covered with soil and planted with native vegetation, with rocks and water-collection points added to create a habitat that allows wildlife to cross in surroundings as familiar as possible. Mangroves, too, have found a "new home." According to project officials, 19.8 kilometers of disturbed areas outside the project boundary are being protected in situ. For mangroves within the project boundary that could not be preserved, 9,572 trees were transplanted to nearby locations, while 275,000 trees were restored elsewhere across an area three times the original size, covering 32.3 hectares. During construction, 966 hectares of mangroves were cleaned and 156 hectares treated for pests and diseases. Today, the number of bird species in the mangrove reserve has risen from 28 to 34, and an ecological corridor is largely in place. From a shorter shipping route to the clustering of industries, from new homes to improved livelihoods, and from a restored fish passage to the renewal of mangrove forests, these three dimensions together show the Pinglu Canal's broader benefits. The canal connects rivers with the sea, but more importantly, it connects development, people's livelihoods and ecological conservation. Copyright © 2026 People's Daily Online. All Rights Reserved.

item.title: Beyond expo floor, AI opens new frontiers in China-ASEAN cooperation
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-18
Beyond expo floor, AI opens new frontiers in China-ASEAN cooperation NANNING, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- Wei Qiaomei, a Chinese livestreamer, once struggled to grasp what her Thai customers wanted, though she speaks fluent Thai. Once, ahead of her pitch for a portable fan, AI analyzed Thai e-commerce data and popped up two selling points for her: quiet motors and long battery life. The trial has proven rewarding. Her employer, based in south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, reported a 300 percent sales jump. "Speaking the language isn't the same as understanding the market," said the 23-year-old, noting that AI had transformed her from a mere translator into a market-savvy presenter. Her story reflects a broader shift in relations between China and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), as both sides aim to expand AI's role in bilateral trade, which exceeded 1 trillion U.S. dollars last year. In the first seven months of 2026, China-ASEAN trade rose 24.7 percent year on year to 744.41 billion dollars, Chinese customs data show, as AI use expands in marketing, agriculture, logistics and finance. This photo taken on Sept. 17, 2026 shows a view of the Nanning International Convention and Exhibition Center, the venue for the 23rd China-ASEAN Expo, in Nanning, south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region. (Xinhua/Zhou Hua) FROM SHOWCASE TO APPLICATION The distinction between technology that draws a crowd and technology that delivers real value is central to the 23rd China-ASEAN Expo and the China-ASEAN Business and Investment Summit, slated from Sept. 17 to 21 in Nanning, Guangxi's capital. The event brings together more than 3,400 companies, with Timor-Leste attending for the first time as ASEAN's 11th member and an official co-host. The expo's inaugural "AI marketplace" features about 500 products from more than 70 companies across eight categories, such as wearables, health management, and consumer technology, allowing visitors to test and buy items on-site. "Last year, AI was mostly for show. This year, it is driving sales," said Wang Jicai, secretary-general of the China-ASEAN Expo Secretariat. For Wei, the results are clear. Her company trained its model on ASEAN languages, local preferences, and cultural nuances, enabling it to analyze products, process reviews, and draft localized scripts. Livestream hosts then decide when to pivot, how to handle tough questions, and what to emphasize. "AI didn't replace me. It amplified what I could do," Wei said. Beyond the livestream studio, AI applications are being deployed in several ASEAN markets. In Laos and Cambodia, a platform developed by a Guangxi enterprise and local partners uses satellite imagery, drones, and ground sensors to track pests and guide tropical crop cultivation. The system, built with Chinese technology, local field data and training support, has been tested on more than 20,000 mu (about 1,333 hectares) of crops, said project head Wen Biaotang. Visitors take photos of a humanoid robot performing tea ceremony during the 23rd China-ASEAN Expo in Nanning, south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, Sept. 17, 2026. (Xinhua/Zhou Hua) CROSS-BORDER DEPLOYMENT NARROWS AI DIVIDE In Guangxi's border city Chongzuo, the center for disease control and prevention has partnered with neighboring Vietnamese provinces to deploy a bilingual AI platform for early disease detection. It can slash epidemiological reporting time from four hours to 30 minutes, the project manager said. In Nanning, RunDo, a platform operated by Runjian Co. Ltd., monitors almost 300 megawatts of solar capacity across nearly 3,000 sites in Malaysia remotely, with drones and AI replacing manual inspections. "The platform has boosted maintenance efficiency by over 30 percent, raised power output by up to 5 percent, and cut labor costs by more than 20 percent," said Yang Yexi, marketing manager of the operator's Guangxi branch. Leveraging Nanning's computing infrastructure, ASEAN companies can avoid building large intelligent computing centers and remotely access models and computing power for their business needs, Yang said, whose company has launched more than 80 computing projects across ASEAN. These cases highlight the prerequisites for cross-border AI deployment: computing power, local data, skilled workers, and capable local partners. Guangxi's China-ASEAN Artificial Intelligence Application Cooperation Center has cataloged more than 1,000 potential AI scenarios, opened 279 to developers, set up offices in Vietnam, Laos, and Malaysia, backed more than 30 cross-border projects, and assembled an alliance of 55 companies. To address the low-resource challenge faced by some Southeast Asian languages, a training base in Malaysia has logged more than 1,900 hours of multilingual data annotation, while a six-month regional competition attracted more than 200 teams. Liu Jianmin, a professor at the School of Big Data and Artificial Intelligence of Guangxi University of Finance and Economics, said ASEAN universities, companies, and professionals could contribute to collecting, labeling and updating data if AI models are to work locally. "No matter how accurate a system is, if no one uses it, can afford it, or can keep it running, it remains just an exhibit," Liu said. The challenge is acute for ASEAN's smaller economies. Without collective action, the cost of cybersecurity, data governance, and reliable AI frameworks could deepen an "intelligence divide," said Miguel Marques Goncalves Manetelu, Timor-Leste's minister of transport and communications. This photo taken on Sept. 17, 2026 shows a scene of the opening ceremony of the 23rd China-ASEAN Expo and China-ASEAN Business and Investment Summit in Nanning, south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region. (Xinhua/Cao Yiming) FROM MATCHMAKING TO RULE-MAKING Before the expo opened, an AI system had generated more than 8,000 buyer-seller matches and arranged nearly 2,000 face-to-face meetings. According to the summit's organizers, the system provides real-time tariff and compliance guidance during negotiations, and tracks leads after the exhibition. But, it still can not establish cross-border data protocols, guarantee electronic signatures, or assign liability when an algorithm fails. AI can turn industrial expertise into a service that can be sold and delivered over time, said Meng Shuang, an associate professor of international economics at the Central University of Finance and Economics in Beijing. Companies, she said, will increasingly package hardware, software, models, and long-term maintenance, with competitive advantage extending to algorithms, sector expertise, and local operating ability. This evolution has pushed regional trade into more complex territory: data governance, AI service pricing and billing rules, electronic authentication, and intellectual property. "Cross-border data flows are the lifeblood of AI," said ASEAN Secretary-General Kao Kim Hourn, who called for a trusted, secure, and seamless framework for data exchange. The China-ASEAN Free Trade Area 3.0 Upgrade Protocol, signed in October 2025, sets out a regional framework covering the digital and green economies, cross-border data flows, personal privacy, digital payments, and AI standards. Standardized electronic authentication, interoperable payments, and joint data frameworks would first benefit sectors such as cross-border e-commerce, smart logistics, and industrial inspection, Meng added. Ge Hongliang, a researcher at the School of Southeast Asian Studies at Guangxi Minzu University, said that cooperation among free-trade zones and ports under the upgraded protocol could support investment, data sharing, and intellectual-property protection. To that end, this year's expo is hosting its first high-level dialogue on aligning Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) and China-ASEAN FTA rules. For livestreamers like Wei, it comes down to knowing which fan feature matters most to a customer hundreds of miles away. Copyright © 2026 People's Daily Online. All Rights Reserved.

item.title: Xi stresses sustained efforts to expand, strengthen advanced manufacturing
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-17
Xi stresses sustained efforts to expand, strengthen advanced manufacturing BEIJING, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping has urged sustained efforts to expand and strengthen advanced manufacturing to provide strong support for advancing Chinese modernization. Xi, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, made the remarks in a recent instruction, which was conveyed at a national conference on advanced manufacturing held in Beijing on Wednesday and Thursday. Efforts should be made to ensure both high-quality development and greater security, pursue smart, green and integrated development, and make the country's industrial chains more self-supporting and risk-resilient, Xi stressed. He emphasized the need to accelerate the development of a modernized industrial system with advanced manufacturing as the backbone, and reinforce the foundations of the real economy. Premier Li Qiang, also a member of the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee, delivered a speech at the conference. Xi's important instructions provide essential guidance for developing advanced manufacturing, Li said, noting that China must treat developing advanced manufacturing as a major strategic task, and press steadily to boost its strength in manufacturing. Li stressed that next-generation intelligent manufacturing should serve as the primary direction, with greater emphasis on digital and intelligent empowerment, high-end manufacturing and self-reliance, green and low-carbon development, and cross-sector integration. Efforts should be made to continuously strengthen the innovation capacity, competitiveness and overall strength of advanced manufacturing, Li said. Li called for deepening the "AI plus manufacturing" initiative, stepping up guidance and support for enterprises' digital and intelligent transformation, and consolidating the foundation of intelligent software and hardware. China should also advance the deep integration of advanced manufacturing and modern services, foster service-oriented manufacturing, and cultivate advanced manufacturing clusters according to local conditions. In his concluding speech, Vice Premier Zhang Guoqing, also a member of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee, said China should further implement the initiative for high-quality development of key industrial chains, accelerate the building of a high-quality standards system, continue to address disorderly and irrational competition, and create a sound ecosystem for advanced manufacturing.
